name: West !Xoon
confidence_why: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress. !Xóõ is described separately below; the pattern is the same.

sweep_summary: huaa1248 (East Taa / !Xóõ, Tuu) is not in the catalog. the list of works with stress in the title holds a single item, Downing 2004 (ZASPiL 37, comparative), which was already downloaded and held by the project from an earlier reading today; re-read in full at Sec. 4 pp. 111-112. It is second-hand: it reports that all Khoisan languages are tonal and that no stress description exists in the Khoisan literature, and infers from Traill 1985's consonant-distribution and root-minimality facts that the morpheme-initial (foot-initial) syllable is the strongest in !Xóõ. No first-hand word-stress statement for Taa was obtained; the first-hand candidates (Traill 1985, Traill 1994 dictionary, Naumann 2008/2016, Güldemann 2013 Taa chapter) remain print/paywalled (the compilation checked HathiTrust, archive.org, MPG PuRe; Glottolog, DoBeS Taa and Wikipedia pages carry no stress statement). A dated second-pass note was appended to Recommended coding if one is needed: tone language, no stress description; highest-value acquisition = Traill 1985 (library print).

new_statements.quote: All the Khoisan languages are described as having tone, and I could find no discussion of stress in the existing Khoisan literature. However, recent work points to other evidence for the importance of foot structure in particular Khoisan languages. [...] Traill (1985) reports that most of the 116 contrastive consonants of !Xóõ are only found morpheme-initially. [...] The restrictions on the distribution of consonants and marked vocalic phonation suggest that it is the morpheme-initial (or foot-initial) syllable that counts as strongest in Khoisan languages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: !Xóõ is a tone language (four root tone melodies whose domain is the bimoraic root/morpheme); no word-stress rule is stated in the primary literature. Distributional evidence (full consonant inventory and non-modal phonation only root-initially) points to the root-/foot-initial syllable (first mora of the CVV/CVCV/CVN stem) as the prosodically strong position.
new_statements.exceptions: Downing notes that in Ju|'hoansi (not !Xóõ) some vowel-distribution facts point instead to the second syllable as stronger; loan adaptation (Afrikaans koppie > kóopì) is cited as evidence that the root template is productive in !Xóõ.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the lexical root/morpheme (minimally bimoraic foot), not the phonological word or phrase; statement is second-hand, derived from Traill 1985's description of East !Xóõ (Lone Tree area).
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern East !Xóõ as described by Traill (Lone Tree / eastern dialects, Botswana) = Glottolog huaa1248 East Taa. Naumann 2016 describes the West !Xoon dialect (West Taa, sibling languoid under taaa1242), not huaa1248. Nakagawa 2006, although listed by Glottolog under huaa1248, describes G|ui (Khoe-Kwadi, gwii1239-type languoid) and is irrelevant to Taa stress.

new_statements.quote: Vowels are also distinguished by tonal differences and it has been necessary to impose an ordering on vowels that differ only tonally. The arbitrary ordering is as follows (using a for illustration): a (high)- a (mid-level) - a (mid-falling) - a (low). [p. 12] ... Plural suffixes and noun prefixes are consistently separated from the stem with a hyphen. This not only marks the morpheme divisions involved, but also delimits the domain of the stem tone. [p. 15] ... they are also marked for one of two tonal classes which determine the tones on the concordially dependent forms ... Tonal Class I determines a melody that is level and Tonal Class II determines a melody that falls. [p. 23]

new_statements.relation_note: First-hand source (Traill himself, the author Downing 2004 reports) confirms the existing statement's reading: !Xóõ is described purely in terms of lexical tone and no stress statement is made. It adds first-hand detail on the tone system (four tones on the stem; two noun Tone Classes with level vs falling melodies) but nothing on stress, so it neither refines nor contradicts the catalog's stress record, which is empty.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary treats !Xóõ as a lexical tone language: four lexical tones (high, mid-level, mid-falling, low) carried on the stem, whose domain is delimited by the hyphens that separate prefixes and plural suffixes, plus two arbitrary noun Tone Classes that impose a level or a falling melody over the string of concordially dependent forms. Nothing is said about word stress, accent or prominence: a full-text search for stress, accent, prominen-, emphasi-, intonation, foot and mora finds only English verb glosses ('stress a rope', 'stress (vb.)'), 'foot' as a body part, 'mora' in the bimoraic-vowel notation, and a labial click offglide 'of variable prominence' (rule 24.8, p. 41).
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; on tone, the Tone Class of a plural noun sometimes changes unpredictably or with alienated vs possessed possession (p. 24), and words with an invariant form retain their own lexical tones
new_statements.identity_note: Traill 1994, p. 8: 'There are a number of distinguishable !Xóõ varieties (see Traill (1985)) but this Dictionary only describes the one spoken in the Lone Tree-Kagcae area' (southwestern Botswana, Ghanzi and Kgalagadi Districts, p. 7). This matches the catalog languoid name exactly (Glottolog huaa1248 '!Xóõ, Lone Tree-Kagcae dialect', i.e. East Taa / East !Xoon); rule 24.14 (p. 42) notes a Kagcae-area idiolect feature (plural suffix te pronounced ne).

tone_statements.quote: Traill’s analysis of !X66 is that there are four tone melodies, one of which is a phonolog- ical contour tone (MF), represented as in (24). He notes that the H(F) melody is phonetic- ally contoured, but since there is no contrastive level H melody, it is possible to view this as a level tone. (24) Traill’s (1985, 1994) lexical tone melodies High H(F) /ghui ‘white person’ A Mid M !éo ‘knife’ | Mid falling MF tda ‘a San person’ Low L sdo ‘medicine’

tone_statements.citation: Bradfield, Julian. 2012. Revisiting East !Xoon verb tones. Abstract (2 pp; the PDF itself is anonymised as 'Anonymous, Erewhon', author and affiliation 'U of Edinburgh' from the workshop programme, talk 5) for the Workshop 'Tone: Theory and Practice', Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig, 28-29 September 2012.
tone_statements.quote: Recently, the DoBeS project has been documenting !Xoon, chiefly Western dialects. Naumann (2008), refined in (2009), has argued, with extensive phonetic analysis, that West !Xoon can be accounted for with two monomoraic tonemes H and L. Both verbs and nouns have a monomoraic root (H or L), and the second mora is a class marker or concordial agreement morpheme, also with a tone. Thus the bimoraic word can have tones HH, LH, HL, LL, corresponding quite naturally to Traill's surface tones.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1, third paragraph; footnote 1 and references on p. 2
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: West !Xoon: 2 tonemes (H, L) per mora; East !Xoon surface: 4 (H, M, MF, L)

tone_statements.citation: Miller-Ockhuizen, Amanda L. 1997. A decompositional analysis of Khoisan lexical tone. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 27(1): 153-168.
tone_statements.quote: This paper gives evidence for a decompositional approach for Ju/'hoasi and !xoo. The mora is the tone-bearing unit, since the number of tones in a word is equal to the number of moras. The domain of tonal specification is the morpheme. [...] For these reasons, I claim that the alternative hypothesis, that !x66 [= !xóõ, scanned] has four level tones and some kind of phrasal tone occurring at the right edge of words, is much more appealing. I will assume this analysis throughout the rest of this paper.

tone.says: Sec. 1.3 states, for West ǃXoon, a high/low tone contrast whose prosody is relevant for distinctions within the cross-reference (agreement) system; person and agreement-class markers fall into two tone classes, and Table 1 'Cross-reference marking and tone classes' lists for each class the agreement suffix after an object vs the anaphoric pronoun suffix vs adjective agreement with opposite tones (e.g. tone class I ACL 2i -àn / -án / -́àn, ACL 3i -è / -é; tone class II ACL 2ii -án / -àn / -̀àn,…
